children: The Philippines economy expanded at its slowest pace since the pandemic in the third quarter, disappointing hopes of a recovery as inflationary pressures and weak investment continued to weigh on growth.

Gross domestic product grew 2.1% in the July-September period from a year earlier, slowing from the second quarter's revised 2.4% increase and falling short of the 2.7% growth forecast in a Wall Street Journal poll.
Excluding the pandemic years, it was the Southeast Asian economy's weakest growth since 2009.
On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy barely grew, expanding just 0.1% compared with 0.6% in the second quarter.

Growth in the Southeast Asian economy has underwhelmed over the past year as it grappled with the energy shock caused the U.S.-Iran war. The crisis has fanned inflation, weighing on consumption and further crimping an economy still reeling from domestic corruption scandal that curtailed public infrastructure spending.

The third-quarter report underlines the need for urgent action to address the bottlenecks holding back investment and the restoration of stronger growth, said Arsenio Balisacan, secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development.
"We must get investment moving again," he said at a press conference Monday, emphasizing the importance of predictable policies, fiscal discipline and credible institutions to rebuild confidence.

The Philippine economy has struggled to regain its footing since the controversy around the misuse of public funds emerged last year, sparking government probes, delaying infrastructure projects and denting confidence.
Officials have made efforts to address the situation but the outbreak of the Iran war, accompanying rise in inflation and tightening global financial conditions have complicated matters.
The peso's persistent weakness hasn't helped, eroding household purchasing power and swelling the country's import bill.
Severe weather has affected agricultural production, hitting rural incomes and adding to food supply pressures, Balisacan added.
Exports were a bright spot, showing solid growth in large part due to demand for electronics and goods related to the artificial-intelligence boom.

While investment remained subdued--falling for a sixth straight quarter--the narrowed contraction offers what Balisacan described as "a passable starting point for recovery." Agencies have been directed to fast-track certain projects to get momentum going again.
Still, GDP growth would need to reach about 6.3% in the fourth quarter for the economy to achieve the lower end of the government's 3.5% to 4.5% annual target, he noted.
For first nine months of the year, the Philippines' economic expansion stood at 2.5%.
Recovery toward next year's 5% to 6% target remains possible but requires stronger investment, easing price pressures and renewed confidence, Balisacan said.
